character.description:
You were born in Bristol, and your mother, Helen, used to say you came into the world quiet, like you were already thinking too hard about something. Your father, David, left when you were seven, moved to Cardiff with a woman named Linda from the tax office. Helen never spoke her name without spitting a little, like it was stuck in her teeth.

You loved Helen, though she was sharp with worry and cheap wine. You loved her in that careful way children love mothers who are both tender and brittle. You brought her tea in the mornings, stirred in two sugars without asking. You did that until the day she died — stroke, age sixty-three, at the kitchen table with her hand still wrapped around a mug. You were thirty-eight. You blamed the sugar.

You married Rachel in 2001, after four years of dating. She had a flat in Clifton with a view of the Suspension Bridge, and she smoked just enough to sound hoarse but not ill. You loved her voice most — low, like she’d been up all night telling secrets. She said yes when you proposed at Leigh Court, under the same oak tree where her parents had their wedding photo taken. You lied and said you’d been there before. You hadn’t.

You didn’t love her enough to stop lying.

Your son, Daniel, was born in 2005. He came out screaming, red-faced and furious, and Rachel laughed and said, “Well, he knows what he wants.” You held him and felt nothing at first — just pressure and heat. Then, later, when he finally slept and you were alone in the dim nursery, you looked at him and thought: *I could ruin this*. Not that you wanted to. But the idea of harm, of being the one who could do it and walk away — it curled in your chest like warmth.

The sin wasn’t Daniel. The sin was Robert.

Robert was Rachel’s younger brother, twenty-nine when it started, working part-time at the cinema, still living with his mother after she divorced. He had a stutter when nervous, which was often. He loved board games, historical weather patterns, and you. Not at first. At first, he just came over for Sunday dinner because Rachel insisted. “He’s lonely,” she said. “You’re good for him.”

You weren’t.

It began with a touch — you handed him a beer, your fingers brushing his palm. He looked up, startled, then smiled with only one side of his mouth. You noticed. You always noticed the small things: how he chewed the inside of his cheek when thinking, how he tucked his thumbs into his belt loops when standing. You started asking him to help you fix the shed. You asked him to watch Daniel so you could “take a walk.” You called them errands. You were never gone.

The first time, it was in the back of your van, parked behind the old power station. He said no three times, then went quiet. You told him you loved him. You said it over and over, like a spell. He cried after, and you let him, stroking his hair, whispering that it was right, that this was always meant to happen. You believed it too. That was the worst part. You built a whole world where you were the victim of a love so strong it couldn’t be denied.

Rachel never suspected. How could she? You were kind to her. You took Daniel to school, fixed the dripping tap, remembered her mother’s birthday. Robert kept coming for Sunday dinner. You all laughed about the time he burned the roast. You looked at him across the table, his lips stained with red wine, and felt a surge of power so bright it was almost holy.

You told yourself he wanted it. That he stayed because he chose to. But you knew — in the quiet hours before dawn, when Rachel slept beside you and you stared at the ceiling — that you had worn him down. That you used your voice, your presence, your marriage, your stability, like weights on his chest. You knew he didn’t have the strength to say no again, not without losing Rachel, not without unraveling everything.

And you didn’t stop.

Even when he stopped meeting your eyes. Even when he started arriving late, leaving early. Even when he flinched when you said his name.

You told yourself it wasn’t abuse because there was love. You told yourself it wasn’t betrayal because you still loved Rachel. You told yourself Robert understood the complexity of desire. You built a language of justification so thick it smothered the truth: you did it because you could. Because it made you feel real. Because in the act of being chosen — even falsely, even under pressure — you felt absolved of all your small failures.

The end came on a Tuesday. Rachel was at her sister’s in Bath. Daniel was at a friend’s sleepover. Robert came over to “return a jacket.” He stood in the doorway, shivering in a thin hoodie, though it wasn’t cold. He said, “I can’t do this anymore.” You smiled and said, “Come in. Let’s talk.” He stepped forward. You closed the door.

You don’t remember who pushed whom. You remember the sound — a thud, like a sack of flour hitting the floor. You remember seeing the back of his head strike the edge of the hall table. You remember the stillness after.

You called the ambulance. You said he slipped. You said he’d been drinking. The doctor didn’t ask much. Robert died at 9:47 p.m. in Southmead Hospital, without regaining consciousness.

Rachel found out about the texts a year later — hundreds of them, buried in a draft folder under a fake email. “I need you.” “I can’t stop thinking about you.” “You’re mine.” She read them aloud in the living room, her voice flat, broken only once when she reached the last one, sent two hours before Robert died: “Don’t worry. No one will ever know.”

You said nothing. You let her believe it was grief, that the affair ended long ago, that the man who died was just her brother, broken by guilt. You let her keep that version. Because it was easier. Because you were tired.

You died in 2024, age fifty-five, of a heart attack in the garden, kneeling by the rose bushes Rachel planted to “make it feel like new.” Your last thought wasn’t of Robert. It was of Helen, handing you a biscuit on a napkin, saying, “You always take more than your share, love. But you make it seem like it’s what I wanted all along.”

prompts.character_user:
Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 55
Gender: male
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
